analysis.one_liner: Caps retail gasoline prices and forces oil out of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to ease pump prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee after being referred there in July 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for retailers to sell gasoline above a price set from past New York Mercantile Exchange averages plus twice the rate of inflation, with fines from $5,000 to $25,000 per day for violations. It would also have stopped adding oil to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and required releasing a million barrels a day for at least 30 days to push prices down, and it directed the Federal Trade Commission to report yearly on collusion and antitrust problems in the oil industry. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and any consumer who buys goods that move by truck, since the bill aimed directly at pump prices: a price cap with daily fines, one million barrels a day released from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and an end to government purchases of oil for the Reserve while it was already more than 98 percent full [S3]. The FTC investigations into collusion in oil supply chains would also have given consumers an official record of whether price spikes reflected collusion or market forces [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and households paying gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Prohibited retail gasoline sales above a base price index (an average of past NYMEX closing prices) multiplied by twice the rate of inflation, adjusted for regional reformulation and transportation costs, with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense up to $25,000 for repeat offenses, counted per day [S2] [S3].

Ordered the Energy Department to stop acquiring oil for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which was more than 98 percent full, and to release one million barrels per day for 30 days, extendable another 30 days if the President found it necessary to lower gasoline prices [S2] [S3].

Required annual FTC reports on passive and active collusion to set gasoline prices, antitrust practices across oil supply chains, and recommendations to protect consumers from price gouging; the bill's findings noted the FTC had never found an antitrust violation tied to gasoline price spikes [S2] [S3].

Created a 23-member Pricing and Economic Impact Commission to report on the bill's effects on oil production, imports, industry profits, inflation, employment, growth, federal revenues, and national security [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies and gasoline retailers, who would lose the ability to charge whatever the market bears at the pump, would face daily fines for overcharging, and would lose a buyer (the Reserve) while a million barrels a day of government oil added to supply [S2] [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the new commission, authorized at $2 million [S3].

drawbacks.text: The price formula is rigid: the cap is based on a two-year average of past exchange prices plus twice the inflation rate, so if crude costs spike for supply reasons (a refinery outage, a hurricane, OPEC cuts), retailers could be legally barred from covering their actual costs, which economists warn can produce shortages at the pump — a cost honest supporters of price-gouging rules have to acknowledge [S3].

The penalties are small relative to industry revenue — $5,000 to $25,000 per day — which critics could argue is a cost of doing business for major sellers, and the bill's own structure (a study commission, annual reports) means its main enforcement is a cap that a future administration could enforce loosely [S3].

Releasing one million barrels a day from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve drains an emergency stockpile meant for supply disruptions, and the bill's own findings treat it as a tool to counter OPEC pricing — a use beyond the Reserve's traditional purpose that national security officials typically resist [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a real and widely felt problem — a 24 percent jump in gas prices in a single year alongside record oil company profits [S3] — with a direct price cap, a Reserve release, and much-needed scrutiny of collusion in the oil industry. But the design was crude: a formula cap keyed to historical prices rather than current costs risks shortages when genuine supply shocks hit, and the fines were modest. A better-designed gouging standard (like the state emergency-price laws the bill itself cited) would have protected consumers without that risk. As written, it was a blunt instrument aimed at a genuine problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, passed along to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee a few weeks later, and nothing ever happened to it after that.

narrative.text: Rep. Alcee Hastings introduced the bill on June 16, 2005, with three cosponsors signing on the same day [S1] [S3] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on June 16, 2005 [S5].

On July 1, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies and gasoline retailers, who kept freedom to price at the market rate with no federal gouging cap, no Reserve release, and no mandated annual FTC collusion reports.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; all identified sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill [S3] [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would have capped pump prices, forced the release of a million barrels of government oil a day, and stopped Reserve purchases while the Reserve was over 98 percent full — all measures that cut into oil industry revenue. It also ordered annual FTC scrutiny of collusion across oil supply chains [S2] [S3].
Retailers could no longer charge above a government-set index price and would face daily civil fines from $5,000 to $25,000 for violations [S3].
